"BUILD A MUSIC INDUSTRY LIFE SIMULATOR — VERSION 1

Build a fully playable, interactive music industry life simulator inspired by BitLife, with deeper music mechanics, historical progression, artist management, character customization, and an open-ended lifestyle simulation.

The game should feel like a living music industry spanning the 1970s through the modern internet era. The player should be able to become a legendary musician, establish a record label, sign artists, form musical groups, accumulate wealth, develop rivalries, and build a lasting musical legacy.

IMPORTANT: This must be a functional game, not merely a static interface or a collection of mock buttons. All major gameplay systems should work, interact, and save their progress.

1. MAIN MENU @COMMENT_BODY@ SAVE SYSTEM

When the player opens the game, display a polished main menu featuring:

- Play.
- Start Career.
- New Save Slot.
- Load Career.
- Settings.

Allow multiple independent career save slots.

Each save must preserve its own character, finances, discography, relationships, businesses, vehicles, properties, and progression.

2. CHARACTER CREATION

When starting a new career, allow the player to choose:

- First name.
- Last name.
- Stage name.
- Birth date.
- Starting year.
- Starting location.
- Initial character appearance.

The player should have both a real name and an artist name.

After character creation, the player enters the main dashboard.

Character customization must remain available throughout the entire career.

3. HISTORICAL PROGRESSION

The player begins their career in a chosen historical year, with the 1970s as the earliest starting era.

Progress through:

- 1970s.
- 1980s.
- 1990s.
- 2000s.
- 2010s.
- 2020s.
- Future decades where appropriate.

Every decade introduces historically appropriate:

- Music trends.
- Technology.
- Recording equipment.
- Distribution methods.
- Industry developments.
- Vehicles.
- Fashion collections.
- Artists.
- Cultural events.

The internet should emerge naturally during the appropriate historical period, followed by digital downloads, streaming, social media, and modern music promotion.

The music industry must evolve as time advances.

4. REAL ARTISTS @COMMENT_BODY@ PROCEDURAL ARTISTS

Include recognizable real-world musicians from different historical generations.

Artists must appear during appropriate eras and develop naturally over time.

For example:

- 1970s soul and funk artists.
- 1980s R@COMMENT_BODY@B, soul, and New Jack Swing artists.
- 1990s R@COMMENT_BODY@B and hip-hop artists.
- 2000s contemporary R@COMMENT_BODY@B and hip-hop artists.
- 2010s and modern artists.

Artists should:

- Age naturally.
- Release music independently.
- Sign record deals.
- Collaborate with other musicians.
- Form groups.
- Experience career success or decline.
- Retire.
- Eventually pass away.

When artists retire or disappear, introduce procedurally generated musicians called REGens.

REGens should possess unique:

- Names.
- Stage names.
- Ages.
- Genres.
- Personalities.
- Careers.
- Discographies.
- Popularity.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.

The industry must never become empty.

Real artists and fictional artists should coexist.

5. MUSIC CREATION SYSTEM

Music must be the central gameplay mechanic.

Allow players to create:

- Songs.
- Singles.
- EPs.
- Albums.
- Extended projects.
- Deluxe albums.
- Compilation albums.
- Group albums.

Every release should contain configurable attributes such as:

- Song title.
- Genre.
- Producer.
- Featured artist.
- Release date.
- Recording quality.
- Promotion.
- Production budget.

Genres should include:

- R@COMMENT_BODY@B.
- Soul.
- New Jack Swing.
- Hip-Hop.
- Rap.
- Funk.
- Disco.
- Pop.
- Neo-Soul.
- Contemporary R@COMMENT_BODY@B.
- Alternative R@COMMENT_BODY@B.
- Gospel.
- Rock.
- Jazz.

Players should be able to collaborate with artists, producers, and songwriters.

Songs should generate sales, streams, popularity, chart positions, and royalties over time.

6. DYNAMIC BILLBOARD @COMMENT_BODY@ MUSIC CHARTS

Implement functioning music charts.

Include:

- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre-specific charts.
- Artist rankings.
- Global charts where appropriate.

Charts must contain numerous competing artists, not just the player.

Every simulated week:

- New releases enter charts.
- Songs rise or fall.
- Older songs gradually decline.
- Viral songs can unexpectedly rise.
- Successful songs can remain charting for multiple weeks.
- Artists compete for positions.
- Popularity and promotional activities influence chart performance.

The player should be able to achieve:

- Top 100 entries.
- Top 10 entries.
- Number One singles.
- Number One albums.
- Gold certifications.
- Platinum certifications.
- Multi-Platinum certifications.
- Diamond certifications.

Chart positions should influence Heat, popularity, record deals, and career opportunities.

7. HEAT SYSTEM

Introduce a dynamic mechanic called HEAT.

Heat represents the player's popularity, commercial momentum, cultural influence, and industry relevance.

Higher Heat should:

- Attract better record deals.
- Increase contract offers.
- Unlock major collaborations.
- Improve concert bookings.
- Increase media attention.
- Improve industry recognition.
- Increase demand for performances.

Heat should rise and fall based on releases, chart success, promotions, performances, controversies, and career activity.

Inactive musicians should gradually lose Heat.

8. RECORD LABEL @COMMENT_BODY@ BUSINESS SYSTEM

Allow players to establish their own record labels.

Label management should include:

- Label name.
- Label logo.
- Signing artists.
- Artist contracts.
- Recording budgets.
- Release schedules.
- Label finances.
- Royalties.
- Promotion.
- Staff.
- Producers.
- Songwriters.
- Artist management.
- Label expansion.

Artists signed to the player's label should have independent careers.

They should release songs, gain popularity, generate revenue, and develop their own relationships and rivalries.

Allow players to receive offers from existing record labels.

Players should be able to negotiate:

- Signing bonuses.
- Advances.
- Royalties.
- Contract duration.
- Creative control.
- Ownership rights.

The player must be able to become an independent artist, a signed artist, or a record label owner.

9. ARTIST RELATIONSHIPS @COMMENT_BODY@ RIVALRIES

Every artist should have an evolving relationship system.

Relationship categories:

- Acquaintance.
- Friend.
- Close Friend.
- Collaborator.
- Mentor.
- Rival.
- Enemy.
- Industry Associate.

Allow players to:

- Meet artists.
- Develop friendships.
- Collaborate.
- Feature artists on songs.
- Produce music for other artists.
- Start rivalries.
- Respond to criticism.
- Compete for chart positions.
- Resolve rivalries.
- Maintain long-term competitive relationships.

Artists should also independently initiate relationships and rivalries.

Rivalries should influence news coverage, popularity, collaborations, fan reactions, and career opportunities.

10. GROUPS @COMMENT_BODY@ BANDS

Allow players to create musical groups.

Players should be able to:

- Recruit members.
- Form duos.
- Create bands.
- Establish supergroups.
- Select group names.
- Manage group members.
- Release group singles.
- Release group albums.
- Share royalties.
- Experience creative disagreements.
- Break up.
- Reunite.

Members can be real historical artists or procedurally generated musicians, provided the timeline is appropriate.

Groups should have independent popularity, discographies, and careers.

11. CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION @COMMENT_BODY@ CLOTHING

Character customization must be extensive and accessible at any time.

Allow customization of:

- Skin tone.
- Hairstyles.
- Facial features.
- Clothing.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.

The player must be able to purchase clothing and permanently retain purchased items.

Clothing categories include:

- Shirts.
- Jackets.
- Trousers.
- Shoes.
- Hats.
- Coats.
- Complete outfits.
- Luxury fashion.
- Streetwear.
- Vintage fashion.

Fashion must NOT be restricted to the current decade.

A player in the 1970s can wear modern-inspired clothing.

A player in the 2000s can wear 1990s-inspired clothing.

A player in 2026 can wear 1980s fashion.

Historical availability should influence the shopping catalog, but the player must retain complete freedom over their aesthetic.

Include a clothing store, outfit builder, saved outfits, and permanent wardrobe inventory.

12. JEWELRY @COMMENT_BODY@ ACCESSORIES

Create a dedicated jewelry shopping system.

Allow purchases of:

- Chains.
- Necklaces.
- Rings.
- Watches.
- Bracelets.
- Earrings.
- Luxury accessories.

Jewelry should be permanently added to the player's collection.

Players should be able to equip, unequip, and combine accessories with outfits.

13. TATTOOS

Allow players to purchase tattoos and customize their character with them.

Include:

- Tattoo designs.
- Tattoo placement.
- Multiple tattoos.
- Tattoo collections.
- Optional tattoo removal.

Tattoos should remain part of the character unless removed.

14. AUTOMOTIVE SYSTEM

Create a dedicated automotive shopping tab.

Vehicles should be historically appropriate to their release years.

Include:

- Classic cars.
- Luxury sedans.
- Sports cars.
- SUVs.
- Supercars.
- Vintage vehicles.

Cars should become available during appropriate historical periods.

Vehicles purchased in earlier decades must remain permanently in the player's garage.

For example, a car purchased in 1992 remains owned in 2026.

Players should be able to:

- Purchase cars.
- View their garage.
- Collect vehicles.
- Sell vehicles.
- Maintain their collection.

Once a vehicle's historical availability period ends, it should no longer be available for new purchases, but existing owners retain theirs.

15. REAL ESTATE @COMMENT_BODY@ LIFESTYLE

Create a dedicated Lifestyle section.

Include:

- Apartments.
- Houses.
- Mansions.
- Luxury estates.
- Recording studios.
- Commercial properties.

Players should be able to:

- Purchase properties.
- Own multiple properties.
- Sell properties.
- View property portfolios.
- Generate rental income where appropriate.

Properties should remain owned across decades unless sold.

16. FINANCIAL @COMMENT_BODY@ NET WORTH SYSTEM

Implement a comprehensive financial system.

Track:

- Cash.
- Music royalties.
- Streaming revenue.
- Sales revenue.
- Touring revenue.
- Label revenue.
- Investments.
- Property ownership.
- Vehicle collections.
- Expenses.
- Taxes.
- Contracts.
- Net worth.

Net worth should reflect actual financial assets and liabilities rather than cash alone.

Allow players to become millionaires, multimillionaires, or billionaires through music and business.

17. MAIN DASHBOARD @COMMENT_BODY@ INTERFACE

Create a modern, polished, interactive dashboard.

The main screen should prominently display the player's character.

At the top of the dashboard, show:

- Character name.
- Stage name.
- Age.
- Current year.
- Current week.
- Energy.
- Heat.
- Cash.
- Net worth.

Underneath the character, display:

- Career status.
- Current popularity.
- Latest releases.
- Chart positions.
- Achievements.
- Career milestones.
- Upcoming opportunities.

Below the career overview, display a continuously updating MUSIC INDUSTRY NEWS FEED.

The news feed should contain headlines about artists, record labels, chart movements, rivalries, awards, releases, industry developments, and historical events.

18. NAVIGATION TABS

Implement permanent navigation tabs.

MUSIC:

- Create Songs.
- Singles.
- Albums.
- EPs.
- Discography.
- Collaborations.
- Groups.
- Recording Studio.

BUSINESS:

- Record Labels.
- Artist Management.
- Sign Artists.
- Contracts.
- Label Finances.
- Investments.

CHARTS:

- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre Charts.
- Artist Rankings.
- Certifications.

INDUSTRY:

- News.
- Artists.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.
- Awards.
- Events.

CLOTHING:

- Clothing Store.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.
- Wardrobe.
- Outfit Customization.

LIFESTYLE:

- Real Estate.
- Automotives.
- Garage.
- Property Portfolio.
- Luxury Purchases.

CHARACTER:

- Appearance.
- Biography.
- Career Statistics.
- Relationships.
- Achievements.
- Net Worth.

19. ENERGY POINTS SYSTEM

Implement a weekly Energy Points system.

The player begins each week with 100 EP.

Activities consume energy.

Example costs:

- Create a Song: 10 EP.
- Record a Song: 10 EP.
- Promote a Release: 5 EP.
- Collaborate with an Artist: 10 EP.
- Attend an Industry Event: 5 EP.
- Perform a Concert: 15 EP.
- Business Activities: Variable EP.

Energy prevents players from completing unlimited activities in a single week.

Activities should have meaningful differences in cost and reward.

Energy should encourage strategic decisions without becoming unnecessarily restrictive.

20. NEXT WEEK SYSTEM

The main progression button should be NEXT WEEK.

When clicked, the game advances exactly one simulated week.

During weekly progression:

1. Process music releases.
2. Calculate streams and sales.
3. Update music charts.
4. Calculate royalties and revenue.
5. Update record label finances.
6. Update artist relationships.
7. Update rivalries.
8. Generate music industry headlines.
9. Process random events.
10. Update Heat.
11. Update popularity.
12. Calculate expenses and net worth.
13. Display a weekly financial and career report.
14. Restore Energy to 100 EP.

After the report, the player returns to the dashboard with a fresh week of activities.

21. WEEKLY REPORT SYSTEM

Every completed week should generate a detailed report.

Display:

- Streams gained.
- Sales generated.
- Chart movements.
- Certifications earned.
- Revenue received.
- Expenses paid.
- Net worth changes.
- Heat changes.
- Rivalry developments.
- Artist relationship updates.
- Industry headlines.
- Career opportunities.

Reports should be dynamic and reflect the player's actual activities.

22. MUSIC INDUSTRY NEWS SYSTEM

Create a dynamic news generator.

News categories include:

- Artist releases.
- Chart updates.
- Record deals.
- Artist signings.
- Rivalries.
- Collaborations.
- Group formations.
- Group breakups.
- Awards.
- Retirements.
- Deaths.
- Industry acquisitions.
- Label expansions.
- Unexpected commercial successes.

News should reflect actual simulated events.

Do not repeatedly display identical generic headlines.

23. RANDOM EVENTS @COMMENT_BODY@ ANTI-REPETITION

The game must avoid repetitive gameplay.

Introduce a dynamic event system that creates unpredictable situations.

Possible events:

- A record label offers a contract.
- An artist requests a collaboration.
- A rival challenges the player.
- A song unexpectedly becomes popular.
- A group experiences creative disagreements.
- A producer offers a unique opportunity.
- A record label wants to sign one of the player's artists.
- A music award nomination arrives.
- A major artist announces retirement.
- An independent musician becomes a breakout star.

Events should provide meaningful choices and consequences.

The game should never rely solely on repetitive button clicking to increase statistics.

24. GAME DESIGN PRINCIPLES

The game must prioritize:

- Freedom.
- Historical immersion.
- Replayability.
- Meaningful progression.
- Dynamic industry behavior.
- Player creativity.
- Persistent ownership.
- Evolving relationships.
- Functional systems.

Players must never be forced into a specific genre, fashion aesthetic, business strategy, or career path.

The player should be able to focus on music, business, lifestyle, or a combination of all three.

25. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

Build a fully functional game with:

- Persistent save data.
- Multiple career slots.
- Working navigation.
- Functional shopping systems.
- Functional music creation.
- Working charts.
- Working finances.
- Working record labels.
- Working relationships.
- Working rivalries.
- Working weekly progression.
- Working Energy Points.
- Functional artist generation.
- Historical progression.
- Dynamic news.
- Realistic simulation logic.

Use a modular architecture so additional features can be introduced in future versions.

Prioritize a playable Version 1 rather than attempting to implement every possible feature superficially.

All buttons must perform their intended actions.

All purchases must affect player inventory and finances.

All releases must influence the music simulation.

All weekly events must update the game state.

All major progression must be saved.

FINAL GAME VISION

Create a living music industry simulation where a player can start as an unknown musician in the 1970s, build a career through the decades, become a legendary artist, establish a powerful record label, sign musicians, form groups, create rivalries, purchase luxury items, collect historical vehicles, own real estate, and accumulate generational wealth.

The game should feel like an actual music-industry life simulator, not a repetitive menu-based game.

The player should feel like they are living through decades of musical history while building their own unique legacy.

Build Version 1 with a polished interface, functional mechanics, and expandable architecture.

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.
"

## Objective
- Build a polished, fully playable music-industry life simulator, Version 1, in the existing repository. The checkout had no existing game implementation, so the work began from scratch.

## Requirements
- Implement persistent multiple career slots, character creation, historical progression, music creation and charts, energy-based weekly simulation, artist relationships, labels, groups, customization, shopping, lifestyle assets, finances, news and weekly reports.
- Prioritize a functional, expandable V1; all major actions should affect game state and saves.
- Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions.

## Decisions
- Use a standalone browser game with vanilla HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser `localStorage`; no framework or dependencies were present.
- Use a dark editorial visual style and organize the implementation into `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `game.js`.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added `index.html` with app root and references to stylesheet and script.
- Added `styles.css` with responsive dashboard, navigation, cards, menus, forms, and modal styling.
- Started `game.js` with save helpers, historical eras and artist data, career initialization, dashboard rendering, and music/charts/industry/business/clothing pages.

### Active
- Finish `game.js`: it is incomplete and currently references missing page/modal/action handlers.
- Implement remaining lifestyle and character screens, interactive actions, weekly progression/reporting, save-slot flow, and functional shopping/business systems.
- Validate JavaScript and run the game locally.

### Blocked
- A shell append attempt failed with `Portable shell scanner cannot analyze command: heredoc`; no content from that attempted append was added.

## Next Move
1. Inspect the end of `game.js` and continue adding code using `functions.edit` or `functions.write` in manageable chunks.
2. Complete modal forms and event delegation for navigation, purchases, music, relationships, and weekly simulation.
3. Run a syntax check, fix issues, and verify core gameplay in a browser if available.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Standalone browser game entry point.
- `styles.css`: Responsive visual design and component styles.
- `game.js`: Partial game implementation; primary file to continue.

## Important Context
- Repository exploration found no app source, package scripts, or framework. Existing `start.sh` delegates to an external runtime, not a local app.
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The current `game.js` ends after `clothingPage()` and is not yet a complete runnable game.
